title: Brownian motion and Itô’s lemma
question: Does the stock move like the textbook model, and what does Itô’s lemma predict for it?

findings: MSFT has an annual volatility σ = 26,4 %. Itô's lemma says this opens a gap of σ²/2 = 3,5 % pts between the average and the compound return (volatility drag); in the data the gap is 3,5 % — in line with the theory.
The model puts the price after 12 months in 327,85 $ – 780,85 $ with 90% probability. The median (505,96 $) sits below the mean (523,88 $): the typical path grows σ²/2 slower than the average one.
Across 10,000 simulated paths the average log return is −3,5 %; Itô's formula gives −3,5 %, while ordinary calculus without the Itô term would say 0,0 %.
Assumption tests: 5 of 9 reject Brownian motion (most clearly fat tails: excess kurtosis 11,6, days beyond 4σ 84× the normal rate). The model describes ordinary days well and extreme days badly.

Out-of-sample test (107 separate 1-month periods, each using only the previous year): the 90% range caught 92,5 % of the moves (standard error ±2,9 pts); in line with what it promises. Breaks below 2,8 %, above 4,7 % (5% each expected).

Applying Itô's lemma to an option price gives the Black–Scholes equation. With the historical σ a 12-month at-the-money call is worth 12,7 % of the price; call + put 20,8 % (shortcut 0.8 σ √T = 21,1 %). Market prices use implied volatility; compare with the Implied move analysis.
notes: Model: dS = μ S dt + σ S dW. Itô's lemma for f = ln S: d ln S = (μ − σ²/2) dt + σ dW, because (dW)² = dt. Solution: S_T = S₀ exp((μ − σ²/2) T + σ W_T); log returns are normal and prices log-normal.
Data: daily adjusted closes over the last 3 years (2023-11-13 – 2026-11-13, 753 returns). The out-of-sample test uses up to 10 years; each month's σ comes from the previous 252 days only.
Zero edge: μ = 0, so the expected price equals today’s and the median sits at e^(−σ²T/2) times it. Past returns are not carried forward (switch on "Use the historical drift" to change that).

Variance ratio: variance of k-day returns / (k × daily variance). Brownian motion predicts 1 (variance grows linearly with time, volatility with √t). Below 1 means mean reversion, above 1 trending. z is the Lo–MacKinlay statistic robust to volatility clustering; |z| ≥ 2 rejects.

Skewness z = skewness / √(6/n), kurtosis z = kurtosis / √(24/n); for days beyond 3σ and 4σ, z is a binomial test against the frequency the normal curve predicts. Jarque–Bera: n/6 × (skewness² + kurtosis²/4), averaging 2 under normality (chi-square, 2 degrees of freedom). Volatility clustering: lag-1 autocorrelation of squared returns; z = ρ √n. Fat tails and clustering are the known weaknesses of Brownian motion; GARCH, jump and stochastic-volatility models were built for them.

Black–Scholes: no dividends, European exercise, constant σ and rate. Rate: US Treasury yield curve, 2026-11-13, matched to each tenor. These are theoretical values, not market quotes. For live option prices, Greeks, the volatility smile and the Heston stochastic-volatility model see #30 Options lab.

Simulation: 10,000 paths, daily steps, fixed seed (same input → same output). The exact solution includes the Itô correction at every step; the naive Euler scheme does not but converges to the same mean.
This is a model test, not a forecast; educational, not investment advice.
